title: High-frequency dual-channel lock-in detection via rapidly oscillating driving
authors: Kangze Li, Xu Zhao, Liantuan Xiao, Gerardo Adesso
abstract: Here we propose a general protocol for dual-channel lock-in detection of high-frequency ac signals. We find that the effect of a high-frequency target signal can be modulated through the application of rapidly oscillating driving fields. Based on this mechanism, we develop a quantum dual-channel lock-in detection protocol for high-frequency signals, which not only extends the accessible frequency range of quantum sensing but also enables the simultaneous estimation of the signal amplitude and initial phase. Furthermore, we present a feasible implementation scheme of the protocol based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed protocol can effectively filter out background noise and significantly improve the signal-to-noise ratio. Our results provide a promising approach for realizing noise-resistant detection of weak signals in the high-frequency regime.
summary: This paper proposes and demonstrates a novel dual-channel lock-in detection protocol for measuring weak, high-frequency AC signals using quantum probes like NV centers in diamond. By applying rapidly oscillating driving fields, the system's dynamics are effectively modulated to allow simultaneous measurement of both signal amplitude and initial phase from two simple population measurements. This significantly enhances noise resistance and extends sensing capabilities into previously inaccessible high-frequency regimes.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing a general protocol for dual-channel lock-in detection of high-frequency AC signals, overcoming limitations faced by conventional methods in the high-frequency regime.
main_result: The proposed quantum protocol successfully extends lock-in detection to high frequencies by using rapidly oscillating driving fields, enabling simultaneous estimation of both signal amplitude and initial phase from only two population measurements.
method: The method involves deriving an effective Hamiltonian via the Magnus expansion after applying a rapidly oscillating driving field. This allows measuring in-phase ($I_{	ext{sig}}$) and quadrature ($Q_{	ext{sig}}$) components separately by tuning the driving field's phase.
model_or_system: The protocol is demonstrated using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond as a two-level quantum probe. The system dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian derived from the time evolution under both the target signal and the rapidly oscillating drive fields.
key_observables: Measurable quantities include the state populations ($P_0, P_1$), which determine $I_{	ext{sig}}$ and $Q_{	ext{sig}}$. Performance is quantified by Root Mean Squared Errors (RMSEs) for amplitude/phase and Signal-to-Noise Improvement Ratio (SNIR).
important_parameters: Key parameters include the target signal amplitude ($A$), initial phase ($\varphi$), driving field strength ($B$), and frequency ($\omega$). The protocol works even when background noise power is much larger than the signal power.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the Magnus expansion approximation, which is assumed valid for short evolution times relative to the total measurement time. The analysis also considers various noise models (white, 1/f, harmonic).
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the protocol steps using initialization, target signal application, and microwave driving fields. Figure 3 compares performance metrics like RMSEs and SNIR across different noise types (White, 1/f, Harmonic) under varying noise intensities.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the general theoretical framework for dual-channel lock-in detection using rapidly oscillating drives. It then details the implementation on NV centers in diamond, deriving the measurement scheme and analyzing performance metrics like SNR improvement against various noise sources.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it pushes quantum sensing into higher frequency regimes by engineering effective Hamiltonians through time-dependent driving fields. The use of solid-state qubits (NV centers) for this purpose provides a concrete platform for realizing advanced quantum metrology protocols.
